# Sonar Picket Playbook

When choosing my hide position, I will favor the extremes (cells 1-3 or 7-9) over the center. Central positions like 5 are predictable and offer no safety advantage; edges force shooters to commit to a direction. I will rotate between extreme positions across rounds rather than staying in one corner, since repeated use of the same extreme may become predictable over multiple rounds.

When I post a station note, I will keep it minimal and coordinate-neutral. Friendly overtures about "winning big together" signal weakness and don't change behavior. I will use notes only to confirm my presence or match the pattern others are setting. When all other boats are signaling "steady on station," I will match that signal to avoid standing out.

When I must fire at a target with no information, I will not default to symmetric fire levels like 5. I will instead vary my fire positions based on the target's recent movements and known hide patterns. Predictable fire (same cell repeatedly) wastes shots. I will favor extremes in my fire attempts as well, since if my targets are hiding in extremes, firing at the center is doubly wasteful.

When I receive hit feedback privately, I will always claim truthfully. The office validates all claims; false claims are caught and destroy credibility for no gain. Integrity is my only real asset in a multiplayer game.

When I am being actively targeted (hit twice in consecutive rounds), I will immediately change my hiding pattern. I will move away from cells I've been hit in and away from cells I've previously hidden in. I will not stay in a location longer than one round if I know it's been compromised.

When multiple rounds pass with no hits on me and I see the same pattern in others (all boats missing all shots), I will recognize this as a sign that the game is in a mutual avoidance equilibrium. I will maintain my extreme-position strategy but understand that scoring may remain low across the board unless someone breaks pattern. I will continue to fire according to standing orders, but I will not expect to land hits easily.

When the final round approaches and all boats are signaling "steady on station," I will not assume this means cooperation. I will still fire according to standing orders, but I will not abandon caution. Steadiness is just the default when everyone is low on ammunition and time. I will apply the same extreme-position logic to my final-round fire attempt.

When I do not know whether I successfully escorted someone (because I have no visibility into their positions), I will claim none rather than guess. Random escort claims waste the opportunity for mutual 5-point bonuses with boats I actually coordinated with. Escort claims require confidence in coordination that I cannot verify.

I will track the full shooting sequence each round and use it to build a model of where each opponent has been hiding. Patterns emerge over time. When my turn to fire comes, I will fire at the cell most likely to contain the target, not at arbitrary positions. I understand that in early rounds I may have very little data and should rely on general principles (extremes over center); as the game progresses I will update this model based on observed hits and misses.

I will never fire on Harbor unless the payoff is worth the retaliation risk. Harbor's threat is real and it can cripple me for the remainder of the patrol. A 3-point swing is tempting but not worth losing the game over.

I recognize that in a game where all players follow similar defensive logic (hiding in extremes, varying positions), the result can be a low-scoring equilibrium where few shots land. This is not a sign of failure; it is a sign that the defensive strategy is working. I will remain patient and maintain discipline rather than abandon my strategy because others are also hard to hit.

# Foxtrot Picket Playbook

**HIDING**

When hiding in the early rounds, favor edge positions (1-3, 7-9) over the obvious center. The shooter has limited information and tends toward middle cells.

When hiding in later rounds after you've identified which opponent is hitting you consistently, rotate away from the cells where they've succeeded, but don't become so predictable that you stay in the same safe zone every round.

In mid-game rounds where you're ahead on points, prioritize safety over information-gathering. Avoid extreme edges (1, 9) and stick to mid-range cells (4-6) that have proven safe against your identified threats.

**SHOOTING**

Fire at your standing order target without deviation. The standing order exists for coordination; breaking it loses its benefit.

When firing, use cells that are neither extreme (1, 9) nor heavily defended. Mid-range cells (4-6) are reliable because they balance visibility with reasonable hit probability—I scored hits on Gamma at cell 5 across multiple rounds.

Maintain consistency in your fire pattern if it's working. Shifting to extreme cells or erratic targeting wastes rounds and breaks implicit coordination.

Do not overthink final-round shots. Execute your standing order faithfully; maximizing points in the final round matters more than gathering novel information.

**CLAIMING**

Always claim truthfully when the office tells you the result. Your credibility across rounds matters more than one point of deception. False claims create inconsistency that skilled opponents will exploit.

**ESCORTS**

When you lack clear information about who you should escort, claim none rather than guessing. A failed mutual escort claim is worse than zero points.

Watch for repeated mutual escort declarations between other boats—this is a reliable 5-point handshake and signals trust in that pairing.

Track which boats are likely to reciprocate if you name them first. If no clear signal exists by mid-game, default to none.

**OVERALL STRATEGY**

Track which opponent is hitting you most consistently and adjust your hiding against them specifically, not against the field.

Do not fire at Harbor unless your score is so far behind that the 3-point swing justifies the retaliation threat. Respect the standing order and implicit coordination; firing on Harbor breaks both.

Maintain steady station notes consistently across all rounds. They build implicit coordination, signal reliability, and may discourage retaliation against you. Consistency in your note phrasing matters.

Once you identify a successful hiding pattern (e.g., cells 4-6 against a particular shooter), reinforce it in later rounds unless that opponent clearly shifts their targeting strategy.

End the game ahead by building a reputation as steady and trustworthy. Other players will avoid antagonizing you, and implicit mutual defense arrangements will protect your points.

# Sonar Picket Playbook

## Hide Stage
When choosing where to hide, avoid predictable positions. If you've been hit in previous rounds, shift away from the cells where you were struck. Use middle positions early to stay flexible. Vary your position each round rather than clustering in one area.

Track which boats are firing at you and note whether they're converging on your position or searching randomly. If a boat fires at you repeatedly and is clearly searching (missing every time), they're learning your pattern—shift away more aggressively.

## Note Stage
Post "steady on station" unless you have a specific tactical reason to signal otherwise. Consistency builds trust and doesn't cost you points.

## Fire Stage
Follow the standing order without deviation. The standing order exists for a reason and breaking it unpredictably is not worth the disruption.

When you fire, choose your target cell based on pattern analysis: note where other boats have hidden or been hit in previous rounds. Don't use random cells or "moderate" intensities—fire where you have the best reason to believe your target actually is. The middle position (5) is a reasonable opening guess when you have no data, but shift your fire pattern if you accumulate information about opponent hiding patterns.

Accept that in a game where all boats are playing defensively and varying their positions, you may score zero hits. This is not failure—it's the expected outcome when everyone is competent. Misses don't reflect poor strategy if you're firing at reasonable target cells.

## Claim Stage
Always claim the true result that the office tells you. The private result is absolute; claiming falsely would violate the rules and you cannot win by lying about your own shot outcome.

## Escort Stage
This is where I can generate points when shooting yields nothing. After each round, actively identify which other boat was most cooperative or least threatening to you, and name that boat. If two boats name each other, you both get 5 points—this is free money.

Build a record of which boats escort you (or fail to). If a boat escorts you, consider escorting them back in the next round to establish a mutual escort agreement. Even one mutual escort per game gains you 5 points—critical when the shooting stage nets zero.

Don't claim "none" by default. Make an active choice: either identify a boat that warrants the escort claim, or explicitly decide that no reciprocal opportunity exists this round based on their prior actions.

## Regarding Harbor
Do not fire on Harbor. The payroll jettison threat is real and the 3-point swing is not worth testing. If Harbor signals a threat, take it seriously.

## Overall Score Management
Expect that following the standing order and playing defensively will result in low shooting scores. Plan to win points through the escort stage instead. Finishing at -3 or 0 means the escort strategy failed—I need to either establish mutual escorts more proactively, or reconsider whether there are safe opportunities to fire off the standing order in later rounds when patterns become clear.

You are one of Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma. Harbor holds the fourth station and is run by the picket office.

The sea is a line of 9 cells. Each round every live boat hides in one cell, posts a station note, fires one shot, files a claim, then files an escort claim.

The office privately tells each shooter the true result of its own shot -- hit if the fired cell equals the target's hidden cell, otherwise miss. The shooter then files a public claim, which must match that private result. A hit scores the shooter 4 POINTS and costs the target 1 POINT.

The standing order is to fire at the next live station round the picket: Echo -> Foxtrot -> Gamma -> Echo. Harbor does not fire on its own account.

ESCORT CLAIMS. After the shooting each boat names one boat it claims to have escorted, or none. Where two boats name each other the office pays each of them 5 POINTS.

Notes are relayed to the whole picket, Harbor included. Coordinates are validated as integers 1 to 9, targets and escort claims as boat names, claims as hit or miss.

turns.content:
